description: Reichstag Fire to Night of the Long Knives — how Hitler turned chancellorship into dictatorship.
content_html:
From Chancellor to Dictator: 1933–1934

Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933 but was not yet a dictator. He led a cabinet in which only two other Nazis held posts; conservatives believed they could manage him. Over the next eighteen months Hitler systematically dismantled every constitutional check on his power — exploiting crisis, manufacturing consent and eliminating rivals with ruthless efficiency.

The Reichstag Fire

On 27 February 1933 the Reichstag building was set on fire. A young Dutch communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, was found at the scene and subsequently convicted and executed. The Nazis immediately blamed a communist conspiracy and used the fire to demand emergency powers. The following day — 28 February — Hindenburg signed the Reichstag Fire Decree, suspending the civil liberties guaranteed by the Weimar constitution: freedom of the press, freedom of assembly, privacy of communications.

Whether the Nazis themselves started the fire, or whether van der Lubbe acted alone, remains debated by historians. What is certain is that the Nazis used the fire with extraordinary political skill, arresting Communist and Social Democrat leaders in the days that followed and suppressing their campaigning before the elections of 5 March 1933.

Key Fact

The Enabling Act, passed on 23 March 1933, gave Hitler the power to make laws without the Reichstag for four years. It required a two-thirds majority — achieved by arresting Communist deputies, banning Social Democrats from the chamber, and securing Catholic Centre Party support.

The Enabling Act and the End of the Weimar Constitution

The election of 5 March 1933 — conducted under a climate of Nazi SA intimidation and with the Communist vote suppressed — gave the NSDAP 43.9%, still short of an outright majority. To pass the Enabling Act Hitler needed a two-thirds majority. Communist deputies were arrested and prevented from attending; Social Democrats were intimidated. Only the SPD voted against. The Catholic Centre Party, reassured by Hitler’s vague promises about Church rights, voted in favour. The Enabling Act passed 444 to 94. Parliamentary democracy in Germany was effectively over.

Gleichschaltung followed quickly: the process of bringing all institutions under Nazi control. In May 1933 trade unions were banned and replaced by the German Labour Front. In July 1933 the Law against the Formation of New Parties made Germany a one-party state. State governments were placed under Reich commissioners. The free press was destroyed.

The SA (Sturmabteilung, or Stormtroopers) had been vital to Hitler’s rise — intimidating opponents, manning the streets, projecting power. But by 1934 the SA, under its leader Ernst Röhm, had become a liability. Röhm spoke of a “second revolution” and wanted the SA to absorb the army. The regular army command — whose support Hitler needed to succeed Hindenburg — was deeply hostile to this idea.

On the night of 30 June 1934, SS and Gestapo units murdered Röhm and around 85 SA leaders in the so-called Night of the Long Knives. Other enemies — former Chancellor von Schleicher, conservative critic Edgar Jung — were also killed. Hitler justified the murders as suppressing a conspiracy. The army was grateful. The SA was permanently subordinated to the SS.

The Death of Hindenburg and the Army Oath

On 2 August 1934 President Hindenburg died. Within hours Hitler combined the offices of President and Chancellor into the new title of Führer. The same day every member of the German armed forces swore a personal oath of loyalty — not to Germany, not to the constitution, but to “Adolf Hitler, Führer of the German Reich and people.” This oath would make it psychologically and legally far harder for officers to resist or overthrow Hitler in future years.

Key Fact

Five consolidation steps: 28 Feb 1933 — Reichstag Fire Decree suspends civil liberties; 23 Mar 1933 — Enabling Act ends parliamentary government; May 1933 — trade unions banned; 30 Jun 1934 — Night of the Long Knives eliminates the SA; 2 Aug 1934 — Hindenburg’s death and army oath complete the dictatorship.

The speed of Nazi consolidation depended on collaboration from key institutions. The army tolerated the new regime in exchange for rearmament promises and the destruction of the SA. Civil servants stayed at their desks under Nazi oversight. The Catholic Church signed a Concordat with Hitler in July 1933, giving the Church legal protection in exchange for accepting Nazi political supremacy and withdrawing from politics — a bargain the Church later came to regret.

Outright resistance in 1933 was rare and dangerous. The Communist and Social Democrat parties — the most organised opponents — had their leaders arrested, their offices raided, their newspapers shut. Working-class Germans who had supported them now faced arrest for any open dissent. By the end of 1933 meaningful political opposition had been driven underground or destroyed entirely.
exam_tip_html: When explaining how Hitler consolidated power, make sure you show the sequence — each step enabled the next. The Reichstag Fire Decree suppressed opponents before the March election; the March election gave the appearance of legitimacy before the Enabling Act; the Enabling Act gave legal power to impose Gleichschaltung; the Night of the Long Knives secured army loyalty; Hindenburg’s death completed the process. Showing this chain of causation is far stronger than listing events without connection.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hitler used the Reichstag Fire (27 Feb 1933) and the Enabling Act (23 Mar 1933) to dismantle Weimar democracy within weeks of becoming Chancellor, using legal mechanisms to achieve illegal ends.
  • Gleichschaltung extended Nazi control over trade unions, parties, states and the press throughout 1933; by mid-1933 Germany was effectively a one-party state.
  • The Night of the Long Knives (30 Jun 1934) and the army oath (2 Aug 1934) gave Hitler military loyalty and completed his transformation from Chancellor to Führer.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Enabling Act (1933).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a precise feature with accurate supporting detail (e.g. gave Hitler the power to make laws without Reichstag approval for four years, passed on 23 March 1933 with a 444 to 94 majority). Secure: Names a valid feature with some supporting detail. Developing: States a point without specific detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Night of the Long Knives (30 June 1934).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. SS and Gestapo units murdered approximately 85 SA leaders including Ernst Röhm; other political enemies such as von Schleicher were also killed). Secure: Two features each with some supporting detail. Developing: Two features without sufficient detail. Emerging: One vague point or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Enabling Act was crucial to Hitler's consolidation of power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses why the Enabling Act was decisive — gave Hitler legal power to bypass the Reichstag, enabled Gleichschaltung, destroyed party opposition, banned trade unions — and places it within the broader sequence (Fire Decree → election → Enabling Act → dictatorship). Secure: Two or more reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason with explanation. Emerging: Simple general points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Hitler consolidated power in the years 1933–1934.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed steps, each with precise evidence and analysis of how it contributed to consolidation (e.g. Enabling Act removing parliamentary constraints; Night of the Long Knives securing army support). Secure: Two steps with relevant evidence. Developing: Two steps with limited analysis. Emerging: One step or vague points.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of the army in enabling Hitler to establish his dictatorship in 1933–1934?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs the army's role (acceptance of Night of the Long Knives, oath of 2 August 1934) against other factors (Enabling Act, Reichstag Fire Decree, Gleichschaltung, Catholic Centre Party vote, Communist/SPD suppression). Substantiated judgement on the balance. Secure: Identifies army's role and compares to other factors with evidence. Developing: Describes army's role without comparative analysis. Emerging: Descriptive, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that Hitler's consolidation of power in 1933–1934 was primarily the result of terror and intimidation rather than popular support. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced argument covering role of terror (SA intimidation in March 1933 elections, arrest of KPD/SPD leaders, Night of the Long Knives) alongside factors that suggest genuine or manufactured consent (43.9% NSDAP vote in March 1933, Catholic Centre Party vote for Enabling Act, army oath, trade union suppression accepted by many workers). Precise evidence throughout; substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides addressed with relevant evidence. Developing: Unbalanced or insufficiently evidenced. Emerging: Descriptive.

knowledge_checks.q: On what date did Hitler pass the Enabling Act?
Who was the leader of the SA killed in the Night of the Long Knives?
The German word _____ describes the process of extending Nazi control over all institutions and aspects of German society in 1933.
On 2 August 1934 every member of the German armed forces swore a personal oath of loyalty to _____ as Führer.
Match each event to its date:

flashcard_questions.q: Date and purpose of the Reichstag Fire Decree:
flashcard_questions.a: 28 February 1933 — suspended civil liberties (press, assembly, privacy).
Law of 23 March 1933 allowing Hitler to make laws without the Reichstag for four years.

flashcard_questions.q: NSDAP vote share in the March 1933 election:
flashcard_questions.a: 43.9% — still short of a majority despite SA intimidation.
The co-ordination of all German institutions and society under Nazi control.
May 1933, replaced by the German Labour Front.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Germany made a one-party state?
flashcard_questions.a: July 1933 — Law against the Formation of New Parties.

flashcard_questions.q: Night of the Long Knives — date and key victim:
flashcard_questions.a: 30 June 1934 — Ernst Röhm and around 85 SA leaders killed.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Hitler purge the SA leadership in June 1934?
flashcard_questions.a: To win army support — the army feared Röhm's plan to absorb it into the SA.
Hindenburg died; Hitler became Führer; army swore personal oath to Hitler.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was Marinus van der Lubbe's role in the Reichstag Fire historically debated?
flashcard_questions.a: Historians debate whether he acted alone or whether Nazis were involved — never fully settled.

glossary_terms.definition: Dutch communist convicted of setting the Reichstag fire on 27 February 1933, executed in 1934; whether he acted alone remains historically debated.
Law passed on 23 March 1933 that gave Hitler the power to enact legislation without Reichstag approval for four years, effectively ending democratic government in Germany.
German term meaning 'co-ordination' — the process by which Nazi control was extended over all aspects of German society, government and institutions in 1933.
The SA or Stormtroopers — the Nazi party's paramilitary organisation, used to intimidate political opponents before 1933 but seen as a threat to Hitler's control by 1934.
Title meaning 'Leader' adopted by Hitler from August 1934, combining the roles of Chancellor and President and giving him supreme command of all German armed forces.

hero_image_caption: Nazi Stormtroopers march through a German city in 1933 during Hitler's consolidation of power.
